conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What is a burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Tissue injury caused by thermal, electrical, chemical or radiation energy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What are the two key axes to assess in any burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Depth and extent (percentage total body surface area, %TBSA).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What are the features of a superficial (epidermal) burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Red, dry, painful and blanching, with NO blisters (e.g. sunburn); heals in ~7 days without scarring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What are the features of a superficial partial-thickness burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Pink, moist, blistered and very painful, with brisk capillary refill; heals in about 2 weeks (7–14 days) with little or no scarring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What are the features of a deep partial-thickness burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Blotchy red/white and drier, less painful, with sluggish or absent blanching; it heals slowly — beyond 3 weeks and with scarring — so it is usually excised and grafted.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What are the features of a full-thickness burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: White/waxy/leathery or charred and dry, non-blanching, and painless in the full-thickness area itself because the nerve endings are destroyed. It usually needs surgical excision and grafting (a very small one may be left to heal).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What is the key clinical sign of a full-thickness burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: It is white/leathery, dry and non-blanching, and painless — the loss of sensation is the giveaway. Beware the trap: a full-thickness burn is almost always ringed by partial-thickness burn that is agonising, so these patients still need strong analgesia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What are the adult body percentages in the Wallace Rule of Nines?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back:
• Head 9%
  • each arm 9%
  • each leg 18%
  • anterior trunk 18%
  • posterior trunk 18%
  • perineum 1%

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: How can the patient's hand be used to estimate burn size?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: The patient's whole palm including fingers is approximately 1% TBSA — useful for small/patchy burns.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: Which chart is the most accurate for estimating %TBSA, especially in children?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: The Lund & Browder chart.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: Why is a different chart used for children when estimating %TBSA?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Children have different body proportions — a proportionally larger head and smaller legs.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: Should simple erythema be included when calculating %TBSA?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: No — count only partial- and full-thickness areas, not superficial erythema.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: When is formal fluid resuscitation indicated in burns?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: For burns of 15% TBSA or more in adults (10% or more in children) — some UK units use a 20% adult threshold. Count only partial- and full-thickness areas.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: State the Parkland formula for burns fluid resuscitation.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Classically 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA of crystalloid over the first 24 hours — that is what the name means, and what an exam asking for 'the Parkland formula' wants. UK burn services commonly start lower, at 3 mL × weight × %TBSA, because 4 mL tends to over-resuscitate. Either figure is only a starting estimate, titrated to urine output.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: How is the Parkland volume divided over time?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Half is given in the first 8 hours (timed from the moment of injury) and the remainder over the next 16 hours.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: Which fluid is used for burns resuscitation?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: A warmed crystalloid — Hartmann's solution (Ringer's lactate).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What guides titration of burns resuscitation fluids?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Urine output — aim 0.5–1 mL/kg/h in adults and about 1 mL/kg/h in children (higher, 1–2 mL/kg/h, if there is myoglobinuria). Both under- and over-resuscitation are harmful.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What features suggest an inhalation injury?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back:
• Burns in an enclosed space
  • facial/neck burns
  • singed nasal hairs
  • soot/carbonaceous sputum
  • a hoarse voice
  • stridor or respiratory distress

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What is the key airway management priority in a burn with inhalation injury?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Early intubation — before airway oedema develops and closes the airway.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: How is carbon monoxide poisoning managed, and why is SpO₂ unreliable?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Give 100% high-flow oxygen; pulse oximetry reads falsely normal, so measure carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) on a blood gas.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What suggests cyanide poisoning after a fire, and how is it treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: A high lactate with metabolic acidosis; treat with hydroxocobalamin.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What is the recommended first-aid cooling of a burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Cool running water for 20 minutes (still worth doing up to about 3 hours after injury), while keeping the rest of the patient warm. Never use ice, iced water or greasy substances — they cause vasoconstriction and can deepen the burn.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: Why must the patient be kept warm while cooling a burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: To avoid hypothermia, especially with large burns.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: How should a burn be covered acutely?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: With cling film laid on longitudinally (not wrapped circumferentially) or a clean non-adherent dressing.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What is the first aid for a chemical burn?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Brush off any dry chemical, then irrigate with copious running water for at least 20–30 minutes — considerably longer for alkalis, which keep penetrating. Do not try to neutralise the chemical: the reaction is exothermic and adds a thermal burn. Hydrofluoric acid is the special case, needing calcium gluconate and specialist advice.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What is an escharotomy and when is it indicated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: An incision through the burn eschar, indicated for a circumferential full-thickness burn causing limb ischaemia or restricting chest-wall ventilation. It releases the eschar only — true muscle compartment syndrome, typically after a high-voltage electrical injury, needs a fasciotomy instead.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: Which burns require surgical excision and skin grafting?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: Deep dermal (deep partial-thickness) and full-thickness burns.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: List the criteria for referral to a burns unit.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back:
• Any burn ≥2% TBSA in a child or ≥3% TBSA in an adult
  • all full-thickness burns
  • all circumferential burns
  • any burn not healed at 2 weeks
  • special areas (face, hands, feet, perineum, major flexures)
  • electrical or chemical burns
  • inhalation injury
  • extremes of age or significant comorbidity
  • and suspected non-accidental injury

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: Which burn distribution in a child should raise suspicion of non-accidental injury?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: A glove-and-stocking or clear immersion-line scald with a sharp upper margin and no splash marks — also a history that does not fit the injury or the child's development, or delayed presentation. Do not delay treatment: document carefully, examine for other injuries, discuss with the paediatric team and a senior, and refer to children's social care.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: What is a Curling's ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back: A stress gastric (peptic) ulcer associated with severe burns.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.front: List the major complications of severe burns.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Burns.back:
• Airway obstruction/ARDS
  • hypovolaemic (burn) shock and AKI
  • infection/sepsis (including toxic shock syndrome)
  • hypothermia
  • compartment syndrome
  • rhabdomyolysis (electrical) with arrhythmias
  • Curling's ulcer
  • and later scarring/contractures

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is urticaria ('hives') and what mediates it?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Transient, itchy WHEALS — raised, itchy weals/plaques with a pale centre and erythematous rim — caused by HISTAMINE release from mast cells into the superficial dermis (transient dermal oedema and vasodilation).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is angioedema and how does it differ from urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Angioedema is swelling of the DEEPER dermis/subcutis and mucosa (lips, eyelids, tongue, throat, genitals) from the same process as urticaria but deeper. It causes tightness/pain rather than itch, and can threaten the airway. Urticaria and angioedema often co-exist.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is the underlying mechanism of (histamine-mediated) urticaria/angioedema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Mast cells degranulate and release histamine (± other mediators) → dermal oedema and vasodilation → itchy wheals (urticaria) or deeper swelling (angioedema).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is a key diagnostic feature of the individual urticarial wheal?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Each individual wheal is TRANSIENT, lasting <24 hours, and the rash migrates (new wheals appear elsewhere as old ones fade).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: How long does an individual lesion of angioedema last, compared with a wheal?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: An urticarial wheal lasts <24h; angioedema swelling can last up to 72h.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: Define acute vs chronic urticaria by duration.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Acute urticaria lasts <6 weeks; chronic urticaria lasts ≥6 weeks (occurring on most days).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What typically causes acute urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back:
Often a clear trigger —
  • allergy (food/drug/venom)
  • infection (especially viral URTIs, the commonest cause in children)
  • or contact.
It is usually a clinical diagnosis needing no tests.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What are the two categories of chronic urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back:
• Chronic SPONTANEOUS urticaria (CSU) — no consistent external trigger, often autoimmune (anti-IgE / anti-FcεRI autoantibodies)
  • and chronic INDUCIBLE urticaria — a physical trigger reproducibly causes wheals.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: List the physical triggers of chronic inducible urticaria.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back:
• Dermographism (stroking/scratching the skin)
  • cold
  • heat
  • delayed pressure
  • solar (sun)
  • cholinergic (exercise/heat/sweat)
  • and aquagenic (water).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: List common triggers of acute urticaria.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back:
• Foods (nuts, shellfish, egg)
  • drugs (penicillins, NSAIDs, opioids, contrast)
  • insect stings/venom
  • infections (viral URTIs)
  • and latex/contact.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: By what mechanisms do NSAIDs/aspirin, opioids and penicillins cause urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back:
• NSAIDs/aspirin trigger or worsen it via a pseudoallergic mechanism
  • opioids cause direct mast-cell degranulation
  • penicillins cause it via an allergic (IgE) mechanism.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is the anaphylaxis red flag in a patient with urticaria/angioedema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Urticaria/angioedema PLUS airway compromise (stridor, tongue/throat swelling), breathing difficulty (wheeze/SOB), or circulatory collapse (hypotension) = ANAPHYLAXIS.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: How is anaphylaxis (urticaria/angioedema with ABC compromise) managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 in 1000) into the anterolateral thigh immediately, repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement, plus the Airway/Breathing/Circulation protocol (high-flow oxygen, IV fluids, lie flat with legs raised). Once stable, a non-sedating antihistamine may ease residual skin symptoms — steroids are NOT part of initial treatment. Provide TWO adrenaline auto-injectors and an allergy referral.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What distinguishes bradykinin-mediated angioedema from histamine-mediated angioedema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema occurs WITHOUT urticaria or itch and does not reliably respond to antihistamines, adrenaline or steroids — but if the diagnosis is uncertain or the airway is threatened, still give IM adrenaline: it is unlikely to cause harm, and withholding it in true anaphylaxis is the greater risk. Histamine-mediated angioedema is usually accompanied by urticaria/itch and responds to those treatments.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: How does ACE-inhibitor angioedema arise and how is it managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown → bradykinin accumulation → angioedema (especially lips/tongue/face), which can occur months to years after starting the drug, without urticaria. Management is to STOP the ACE inhibitor permanently and never re-challenge, avoiding the class; if a renin-angiotensin blocker is still needed, an ARB only after full resolution and with counselling. The swelling may take days to settle and can recur for some weeks after stopping.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is hereditary angioedema and its inheritance/cause?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: An autosomal dominant condition due to C1 ESTERASE INHIBITOR deficiency, causing recurrent angioedema WITHOUT urticaria (face, limbs, GI tract → abdominal pain, and larynx).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What biochemical findings screen for hereditary angioedema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Low C1 esterase inhibitor level and a persistently LOW C4 (a useful screening test).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: How is hereditary angioedema treated during attacks?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: With C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant (a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist). Antihistamines, adrenaline and steroids do not reliably work, because it is bradykinin-mediated — though a threatened airway is still treated with adrenaline while the mechanism is being sorted out.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What investigations are appropriate for acute urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Usually none — it is a clinical diagnosis; identify and remove the trigger.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What investigations may be used in chronic urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Usually clinical, with limited screening (e.g. FBC, ESR/CRP, thyroid function/antibodies) if a cause is suspected. Routine extensive allergy testing is NOT indicated, as chronic spontaneous urticaria is usually not allergic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What investigations are indicated for angioedema WITHOUT urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: C4 and C1 esterase inhibitor levels (to screen for hereditary/acquired angioedema), and review of ACE inhibitor use.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is the first-line treatment for acute urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Remove the trigger and give a non-sedating (2nd-generation) H1-antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine). A short course of oral prednisolone (e.g. 40 mg daily for up to 5–7 days in an adult) can be used for a severe acute flare — do not repeat the course, and never use it long-term.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: Outline the stepwise management ladder for chronic urticaria.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back:
• 1st-line: a regular non-sedating (2nd-generation) H1-antihistamine — cetirizine 10 mg, loratadine 10 mg or fexofenadine 180 mg once daily.
  • 2nd: up-dose the antihistamine, doubling it first and going up to 4× the standard dose (off-licence above the standard dose, with the higher end usually on specialist advice), ± a leukotriene receptor antagonist such as montelukast.
  • 3rd, for refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria: omalizumab (anti-IgE monoclonal).
  • 4th: ciclosporin (specialist immunosuppressant).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is omalizumab and where does it fit in urticaria management?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: An anti-IgE monoclonal antibody used as third-line therapy for refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria (after a non-sedating antihistamine and up-dosing to 4×).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: Which associations are linked with chronic (spontaneous) urticaria?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: Autoimmune conditions — notably thyroid autoimmunity and other autoimmune diseases; it is often idiopathic/autoimmune.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.front: What is dermographism?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Ang.back: A form of chronic inducible urticaria in which stroking or scratching the skin reproducibly produces a linear wheal ('skin writing').

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What are the four layers/questions used to describe any skin lesion?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back:
• MORPHOLOGY (the primary lesion)
  • SECONDARY CHANGES (what has happened to it)
  • CONFIGURATION (how lesions are arranged)
  • and DISTRIBUTION (where on the body).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a macule.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A small (<1 cm) area of COLOUR change that is flat (not elevated, not palpable). Examples: a freckle, a small area of vitiligo.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a patch.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A large (>1 cm) area of flat colour change with a smooth surface (not palpable). Example: a café-au-lait patch.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a papule.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: An elevated, SOLID, palpable lesion ≤1 cm in diameter.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a plaque.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A circumscribed, palpable, usually elevated lesion >1 cm — a 'plateau'-like raised area (e.g. psoriasis plaques).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a nodule.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: An elevated, solid, palpable lesion >1 cm located deeper in the skin (dermis/subcutis).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What is the difference between a plaque and a nodule?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Both are raised solid lesions >1 cm; a plaque is a flat-topped, plateau-like elevation, whereas a nodule is deeper (dermal/subcutaneous) and more three-dimensional.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a vesicle and a bulla, including the size cut-off.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Both are fluid-filled blisters: a vesicle is ≤1 cm; a bulla is >1 cm (the same 1 cm cut-off as macule/papule).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a pustule, and is it always infected?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A circumscribed lesion <1 cm containing PUS (neutrophils), appearing white/yellow. It is NOT always infected — e.g. sterile pustular psoriasis or pustular drug eruptions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a cyst and how it differs from an abscess.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A cyst is a papule/nodule containing fluid or semi-fluid material and is fluctuant (often non-infected). An abscess is a localised collection of PUS (infected).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a wheal and which condition it characterises.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A wheal (weal) is a TRANSIENT elevation of skin due to DERMAL OEDEMA — often pale centrally with an erythematous rim and NO surface change. It is the lesion of URTICARIA (individual lesions last <24h; histamine-mediated).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Which primary lesions use the 1 cm cut-off between 'small' and 'large' versions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back:
• Macule (<1 cm) vs patch (>1 cm)
  • papule (≤1 cm) vs plaque (>1 cm)
  • vesicle (≤1 cm) vs bulla (>1 cm).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: List some papule descriptors and what they suggest.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back:
• Acuminate (pointed)
  • dome-shaped (rounded, e.g. intradermal naevus)
  • filiform (thread-like)
  • flat-topped
  • pedunculated (on a stalk, e.g. skin tag)
  • sessile (no stalk)
  • umbilicated (central depression, e.g. molluscum)
  • verrucous (warty, e.g. viral wart).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define scale.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Flakes of stratum corneum, often accentuated by scraping the lesion.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define crust.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Dried PLASMA exuding through an eroded epidermis — rough, yellow/brown (a bloody crust appears red/purple/black).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define an erosion and how it heals.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A superficial, PARTIAL loss of surface tissue (epidermis only) — it heals WITHOUT a scar.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define an ulcer and how it heals.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A FULL-thickness loss of epidermis plus at least part of the dermis (± subcutis) — it heals WITH a SCAR.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What is the key difference between an erosion and an ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Depth: an erosion is partial (epidermis only) and heals without scarring; an ulcer is full-thickness (into the dermis) and heals with a scar.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define excoriation.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Loss of epidermis (± dermis) due to SCRATCHING — appearing as linear or punctate marks; a hallmark of chronic itch.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define lichenification.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Palpably THICKENED skin with increased/exaggerated skin markings and lichenoid scale, resulting from chronic RUBBING (e.g. atopic eczema).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Which two secondary changes are hallmarks of chronic itch?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Excoriation (scratch marks) and lichenification (thickened skin with exaggerated skin lines from chronic rubbing) — e.g. in atopic eczema.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define a fissure and atrophy.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: A fissure is a linear crack or split extending through the epidermis into the dermis — painful and may bleed. Atrophy is thinning of the skin, epidermal (shiny, wrinkled, "cigarette-paper") or dermal (depressed).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define the 'annular' configuration and give a classic example.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Ring-shaped — classically tinea (ringworm) and granuloma annulare.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Which configuration is 'target/iris', and what condition is it classic for?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Concentric rings (a target lesion) — classic for erythema multiforme.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What does a 'grouped/herpetiform' configuration suggest?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Clustered lesions — classically the grouped vesicles of herpes (HSV).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What does 'nummular/discoid' configuration mean and its classic example?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Coin-shaped lesions — classically discoid (nummular) eczema.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What does 'linear' configuration suggest?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Lesions in a line — e.g. the Koebner phenomenon (lesions along a scratch) or contact dermatitis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What does a 'reticular' configuration mean, with examples?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Net-like/lacy — e.g. livedo reticularis and Wickham's striae of lichen planus.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Name the high-yield distribution pairs and their diagnoses.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back:
• Extensor (elbows/knees) = psoriasis
  • flexural (creases) = atopic eczema
  • photosensitive (sun-exposed) = lupus/dermatomyositis
  • dermatomal = shingles
  • seborrhoeic (scalp/nasolabial/central chest) = seborrhoeic dermatitis
  • acral = hand-foot-mouth/acral melanoma.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What does a 'blaschkoid' distribution follow?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Blaschko's lines (developmental lines) — seen in epidermal naevi and some genodermatoses.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Distinguish hypopigmented, depigmented and hyperpigmented.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back:
• Hypopigmented = reduced pigment (e.g. pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory)
  • depigmented = total loss of pigment (e.g. vitiligo)
  • hyperpigmented = increased pigment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Define erythema, purpura and telangiectasia.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back:
• Erythema = blanching redness (vascular dilatation)
  • purpura = non-blanching discolouration from extravasated blood
  • telangiectasia = visible dilated small vessels.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: What is the blanching (diascopy) test and what does it distinguish?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Pressing a glass slide on the lesion: erythema BLANCHES (vascular dilatation), whereas purpura does NOT blanch (extravasated blood). It distinguishes vascular dilatation from bleeding into the skin.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.front: Distinguish petechiae from ecchymoses.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Mor.back: Both are purpura (non-blanching). Petechiae are <2 mm; ecchymoses (bruises) are larger.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is tinea ('ringworm')?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A superficial fungal infection of keratinised tissue (skin, hair, nails) caused by DERMATOPHYTES — moulds of the genera Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton. It is classified by the body site involved.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What do dermatophytes live on, and why does this determine which tissues they infect?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: They digest KERATIN, so they infect keratinised tissues — skin (stratum corneum), hair and nails. Both the appearance and the naming of tinea follow the site involved.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe the classic morphology of tinea corporis.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: An annular ('ring'), scaly, erythematous plaque with a raised, active, advancing scaly EDGE and CENTRAL CLEARING, spreading centrifugally outward. Itchy, and may be polycyclic/serpiginous where rings merge.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is tinea classified, and give the site names.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
By body site:
  • corporis (body)
  • cruris (groin)
  • pedis (feet/'athlete's foot')
  • manuum (hand)
  • capitis (scalp/hair)
  • unguium (nail/onychomycosis)

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the key treatment rule that hinges on the site of tinea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Skin tinea (corporis/cruris/pedis) responds to TOPICAL antifungals; hair (capitis) and nails (unguium) need ORAL antifungals because topicals cannot penetrate the hair follicle or nail plate.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why does tinea capitis require oral rather than topical antifungals?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because topical antifungals cannot reach the fungus within the hair follicle. Oral therapy is needed to eradicate follicular infection.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why does onychomycosis (tinea unguium) require oral antifungals?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because topical agents cannot penetrate the nail plate adequately to eradicate the infection; oral antifungals reach the nail via the nail bed/matrix.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is a kerion, and why must it be treated promptly?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A kerion is a boggy, pustular, inflammatory mass of the scalp seen in tinea capitis. It must be treated promptly with oral antifungals to prevent SCARRING ALOPECIA.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe tinea cruris.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: An annular/polycyclic, itchy, scaly rash in the groin with a serpiginous advancing border that characteristically SPARES the scrotum. Treated topically.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe tinea pedis (athlete's foot) and its treatment.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Itchy scaling and maceration between the toes, sometimes with a moccasin (sole) or vesicular pattern. Treated topically, but oral antifungals are used for severe/moccasin-type disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is tinea incognito?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Tinea that has been mistakenly treated with TOPICAL STEROIDS (as if eczema). The steroid suppresses inflammation but lets the fungus spread, making the rash atypical, less scaly, more extensive and losing its classic ring — so the diagnosis is missed.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the key management trap to avoid in an undiagnosed scaly/annular rash?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Do not treat it with topical STEROIDS — steroids disguise and worsen tinea (tinea incognito). If unsure, take scrapings to confirm/exclude fungus first.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What investigations confirm tinea, and when are they especially indicated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Skin/nail scrapings or plucked hair for microscopy (KOH prep) and fungal culture. For ONYCHOMYCOSIS confirm before starting, because the course is long and hepatotoxic. For CAPITIS and kerion take the samples but start oral treatment empirically without waiting — delay costs scarring alopecia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the role of a Wood's lamp in tinea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Some Microsporum scalp infections fluoresce green under a Wood's lamp, which can help identify tinea capitis (though many dermatophytes do not fluoresce).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the first-line topical treatment for skin tinea?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Topical terbinafine (fungicidal, shorter course) or a topical azole (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole). Keep the area dry, treat any concurrent tinea pedis reservoir, and change socks/underwear.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the first-line ORAL treatment for tinea capitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Oral terbinafine (first-line, especially for Trichophyton) or griseofulvin (traditional; preferred for Microsporum and kerion), typically 4–8 weeks, often with an adjunctive antifungal shampoo (ketoconazole/selenium sulfide). Examine household contacts for asymptomatic carriage and treat carriers. Check LFTs before and during terbinafine; griseofulvin is teratogenic and reduces the efficacy of combined hormonal contraception.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the first-line oral treatment for onychomycosis, and how long is the course?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Oral terbinafine 250 mg once daily — a long course of roughly 6 weeks to 3 months for fingernails and 3–6 months for toenails. Confirm the diagnosis mycologically before starting, and check LFTs before and during treatment.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: When is oral antifungal therapy indicated for SKIN tinea (not just hair/nails)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
When skin tinea is
  • extensive/widespread
  • refractory to topical treatment
  • in an immunocompromised patient
  • or severe (e.g. moccasin-type tinea pedis)

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Which factors predispose to tinea infection?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
• Warm/humid conditions
  • shared facilities (gyms, pools, communal showers)
  • animal contact
  • occlusion
  • immunosuppression and diabetes

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Which conditions can tinea mimic, reinforcing the need for mycological confirmation?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
• Tinea corporis mimics eczema/psoriasis/discoid eczema
  • tinea capitis mimics alopecia areata
  • onychomycosis mimics psoriatic or traumatic nail dystrophy

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why should concurrent tinea pedis be treated when managing tinea corporis or cruris?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because tinea pedis acts as a reservoir that can re-seed infection elsewhere; treating it (and keeping areas dry, changing socks/underwear) reduces recurrence.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the characteristic scalp finding in tinea capitis, and who is most affected?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Scaly patches with hair loss and broken hairs ('black dots'), ± pustules/kerion/favus. It is a key cause of childhood hair loss.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What causes herpes simplex, and what is the characteristic lesion?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Infection with herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 or HSV-2), a DNA herpesvirus. It causes recurrent GROUPED VESICLES on an erythematous base at mucocutaneous sites.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the classic site distinction between HSV-1 and HSV-2?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: HSV-1 = oral/facial (cold sores), and increasingly genital; HSV-2 = classically genital. There is overlap, so type does not perfectly predict site.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe the latency and reactivation cycle of HSV.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: After primary infection, the virus travels up the sensory nerve to establish lifelong LATENCY in the sensory (dorsal-root/trigeminal) ganglion, then periodically reactivates and travels back down the nerve to produce recurrent lesions at the SAME site.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: List common triggers for HSV reactivation.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
• UV/sunlight
  • stress
  • illness/fever
  • immunosuppression
  • menstruation
  • and local trauma

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How does primary HSV differ from recurrent HSV?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Primary infection is often more severe and may be systemic (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy — e.g. gingivostomatitis). Recurrent (reactivation) episodes are milder and shorter, preceded by a tingling/burning prodrome, and occur at the same site each time.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the typical prodrome of recurrent HSV?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Tingling or burning at the site, occurring before the visible vesicles appear.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe herpes labialis (cold sores).
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Grouped vesicles on the lip/perioral skin (usually HSV-1). A prodromal tingle is followed by vesicles → crust → healing over about 7–10 days; episodes are recurrent.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is herpetic gingivostomatitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Primary oral HSV, typically in children — fever, painful oral vesicles/ulcers, gum swelling, drooling, and lymphadenopathy. It is often the most severe (primary) episode.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe genital herpes.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Painful grouped genital vesicles/ulcers (HSV-2 > HSV-1), sexually transmitted. Primary episodes can be severe and systemic; recurrences are milder.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is a herpetic whitlow, and what must you NOT do?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: HSV infection of a FINGER — painful vesicles/pustules on a digit from direct inoculation. Do NOT incise it — it is viral, not a bacterial abscess.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is herpes gladiatorum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: HSV spread by skin-to-skin contact, classically in wrestlers/contact-sport athletes.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is eczema herpeticum and why is it dangerous?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Widespread HSV infection of eczematous/barrier-defective skin — monomorphic 'punched-out' vesicles/erosions with systemic upset. It is a dermatological EMERGENCY: give aciclovir, and ADMIT for IV aciclovir if it is extensive, if the patient is systemically unwell, an infant, or unable to take oral treatment. Any periocular involvement needs same-day ophthalmology.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is herpetic keratitis and how is it managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: HSV infection of the eye producing a DENDRITIC corneal ulcer (seen on fluorescein staining) — sight-threatening. Needs urgent ophthalmology and aciclovir; AVOID topical steroids.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is herpes (HSV) encephalitis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: HSV-1 causing temporal-lobe encephalitis — fever, confusion, seizures. It is treated urgently with IV aciclovir.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How does neonatal HSV arise and how is it treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Usually from maternal genital HSV at delivery. It can affect skin/eye/mouth, CNS, or be disseminated, and is severe — treated with IV aciclovir.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Which skin condition is HSV the commonest trigger for?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Erythema multiforme — HSV is its most common precipitant.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the investigation of choice to confirm HSV when needed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A viral swab of a deroofed vesicle for HSV PCR (test of choice); viral culture and serology have more limited roles. Diagnosis is often clinical.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How are mild recurrent cold sores managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Usually self-limiting — no treatment needed. Topical aciclovir has limited benefit; oral aciclovir/valaciclovir only shortens episodes if started at the PRODROME. Routine treatment of mild recurrent HSV-1 in healthy people is not recommended.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is primary/severe HSV, gingivostomatitis or genital herpes treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Oral aciclovir (or valaciclovir), most effective started early (within 72 hours or at the prodrome), plus analgesia, hydration and supportive care.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is suppressive antiviral therapy and when is it used?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Daily oral aciclovir (e.g. 400 mg twice daily) or valaciclovir for frequent/severe recurrent HSV (e.g. ≥6 genital episodes/year) — it reduces recurrences and viral shedding/transmission. Review/pause periodically.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: When is IV aciclovir indicated in HSV?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
For danger presentations —
  • encephalitis
  • disseminated HSV
  • neonatal HSV
  • severe eczema herpeticum
  • and severe disease in the immunocompromised

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Explain the mechanism and selective toxicity of aciclovir.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Aciclovir is a guanosine analogue activated (phosphorylated) by the VIRAL thymidine kinase, so it is concentrated in infected cells, where it inhibits viral DNA polymerase — giving selective toxicity toward HSV-infected cells.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What general advice reduces HSV spread and complications?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
• Avoid triggers (SPF for UV-triggered labial HSV)
  • avoid autoinoculation (especially to the eyes)
  • and avoid contact with neonates, people with eczema, and the immunocompromised during an outbreak

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is shingles (herpes zoster)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) — the same DNA herpesvirus that causes chickenpox as the primary infection. After chickenpox, VZV lies dormant in a sensory (dorsal-root/cranial) ganglion and reactivates to produce clustered vesicles in a dermatomal distribution.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why is the shingles rash unilateral and band-like, stopping at the midline?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because reactivated VZV travels down a single sensory nerve, so the rash follows one DERMATOME — making it unilateral, band-like, and stopping at the midline.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How does shingles differ from chickenpox in distribution and lesion stage?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Chickenpox = primary, WIDESPREAD/generalised infection with vesicles at DIFFERENT stages (crops). Shingles = reactivation, UNILATERAL along a single dermatome with grouped vesicles at the SAME stage.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe the typical prodrome and evolution of a shingles rash.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A prodrome of dermatomal pain, tingling, burning or itch (± fever/malaise) for days before the rash; then grouped erythematous papules → vesicles → pustules → crust along one dermatome, crusting over ~7–10 days and healing in 2–4 weeks (± scarring/pigment change).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Which dermatomes are most commonly affected by shingles?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Thoracic dermatomes are commonest, followed by trigeminal (ophthalmic), cervical and lumbar.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Is shingles contagious, and how does its infectivity differ from chickenpox?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Shingles can give CHICKENPOX to a non-immune contact via contact with vesicle fluid — localised covered zoster is not airborne like chickenpox, though disseminated zoster and zoster in the immunocompromised are managed as airborne-infectious. Advise covering lesions and avoiding non-immune pregnant women, neonates, and the immunocompromised.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What increases the risk of VZV reactivation (shingles)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Increasing age and immunosuppression — both reflect waning cell-mediated immunity to VZV.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is zoster sine herpete?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Dermatomal pain caused by VZV reactivation WITHOUT a visible rash — a diagnostic trap.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is herpes zoster ophthalmicus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Shingles of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), affecting the forehead/eye, with risk of keratitis, uveitis and sight loss.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is Hutchinson's sign and why does it matter?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Vesicles on the TIP or SIDE of the nose (nasociliary nerve involvement), which predicts eye involvement in herpes zoster ophthalmicus and warrants urgent (same-day) ophthalmology review.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (CN VII) → facial palsy plus vesicles in the ear canal/auricle, ± hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus and loss of taste.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is Ramsay Hunt syndrome treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Antivirals PLUS corticosteroids, with specialist/ENT referral.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What does disseminated zoster (>1 dermatome or widespread) suggest, and how is it managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: It suggests underlying immunocompromise; manage with IV aciclovir and investigate for an immunosuppressive cause.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Persistent neuropathic pain in the affected dermatome lasting >~90 days after rash onset — the commonest complication of shingles.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What are the risk factors for post-herpetic neuralgia?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Older age (the biggest factor), severe acute pain/rash, and ophthalmic involvement.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is post-herpetic neuralgia managed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Neuropathic pain agents — amitriptyline, gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine; topical capsaicin/lidocaine; and specialist pain referral if refractory. Paracetamol/NSAIDs alone are usually inadequate.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the antiviral regimen for shingles and its ideal timing?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily (or valaciclovir 1 g TDS / famciclovir 500 mg TDS) for 7 days, started ideally within 72 hours of rash onset.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: When can antivirals still be started beyond 72 hours of rash onset?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: If new vesicles are still forming, or in older, immunocompromised, or ophthalmic/severe cases — antivirals may be started up to about a week after onset.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Do immunocompetent children with shingles routinely need antivirals?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: No — shingles in immunocompetent children is usually mild and does not routinely require antivirals. Seek specialist advice in pregnancy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is pain managed in acute shingles?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Standard analgesia (paracetamol ± NSAID, stepping up to codeine), with neuropathic agents (e.g. amitriptyline/gabapentin) added for severe acute pain or post-herpetic neuralgia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is the diagnosis of shingles confirmed when atypical or in the immunocompromised?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: It is usually clinical, but can be confirmed with a viral swab of vesicle fluid for VZV PCR.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What vaccine is used to prevent shingles, and what type is it?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A recombinant (non-live), adjuvanted vaccine, given as TWO doses.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Who is offered the shingles vaccine on the UK NHS schedule?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Immunocompetent adults on turning 65, with a catch-up for those aged 70–79; and severely immunosuppressed adults from age 18 (recently expanded down from 50).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why is it significant that the recombinant shingles vaccine has replaced the older live-attenuated one?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because the current vaccine is non-live (recombinant), it is safe in immunocompromised patients, whereas the older live-attenuated single-dose vaccine was contraindicated in immunocompromise.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What advice about contacts should you give a patient with shingles?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Cover the lesions and avoid contact with non-immune pregnant women, neonates and the immunocompromised, since vesicle fluid can transmit VZV and cause chickenpox in a non-immune person. If such a contact has already occurred, that person needs urgent VZV antibody testing and, if not immune, post-exposure prophylaxis with an oral antiviral.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is molluscum contagiosum and what causes it?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A common, benign, self-limiting viral skin infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus, a POXVIRUS. It presents as monomorphic, shiny, dome-shaped papules with a central umbilicated punctum.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe the characteristic lesion of molluscum contagiosum.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Small (1–5 mm), firm, pearly/pink/skin-coloured, dome-shaped papules with a central UMBILICATION (dimple) containing a cheesy/white core. Lesions are monomorphic (all look alike) and often clustered.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How does molluscum contagiosum spread?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: By direct skin-to-skin contact and autoinoculation (scratching spreads it to adjacent skin, producing clusters). It can also spread via shared towels and, in adults, sexual contact.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Who most commonly gets molluscum contagiosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Children (immunocompetent) — it is very common and self-limiting. It is also more extensive in people with atopic eczema, and sexually acquired in adults.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why is molluscum more numerous/widespread in atopic eczema?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because of the impaired skin barrier (and sometimes immunosuppressant treatment), which allows easier spread; scratching promotes autoinoculation. Treating the eczema helps reduce spread.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What does genital molluscum contagiosum in an adult imply?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: It is usually sexually transmitted, so it warrants a sexual health referral and consideration/screening for other STIs.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What does widespread, atypical, or giant molluscum suggest, especially on the face?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Immunosuppression — notably HIV. Widespread/atypical/large ('giant') or facial molluscum should prompt investigation, including an HIV test.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the natural history of molluscum contagiosum in an immunocompetent person?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: It resolves spontaneously over months (up to about 18 months) without scarring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the mainstay of management for typical molluscum contagiosum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Reassurance — it is benign and self-limiting, so no treatment is usually needed. Avoid aggressive treatment, especially in children.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What advice should be given to reduce spread of molluscum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Avoid scratching and sharing towels (to reduce autoinoculation and transmission). Children do NOT need to be excluded from school or swimming.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: When is active treatment of molluscum contagiosum indicated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
Only if lesions are
  • troublesome
  • extensive
  • cosmetically/psychologically distressing
  • or genital in adults

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What treatment options exist for molluscum when treatment is indicated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Cryotherapy, curettage, or topical agents (potassium hydroxide, benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid), used selectively — they can cause discomfort or scarring. Imiquimod is NOT used for cutaneous molluscum: trials showed it is no better than placebo and caused severe local reactions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is molluscum contagiosum usually diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Clinically, from the characteristic umbilicated dome-shaped papules. Further workup (STI screen, HIV test, biopsy) is reserved for the special contexts or diagnostic doubt.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What does biopsy of a molluscum lesion show?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Henderson-Paterson bodies ('molluscum bodies') — intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies. Biopsy is only needed if there is diagnostic doubt.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How should co-existing atopic eczema be managed in a patient with molluscum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Treat the eczema — this improves the skin barrier and reduces scratching, spread and secondary molluscum dermatitis.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How does molluscum respond to immune restoration in HIV?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Widespread molluscum in HIV often improves with immune restoration/antiretroviral therapy, so treating the underlying immunosuppression is key.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is 'molluscum dermatitis'?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A surrounding eczematous reaction (itchy, inflamed skin) that can develop around molluscum lesions; lesions themselves can also become inflamed as they begin to resolve.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How do molluscum papules differ from viral warts?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Molluscum papules are smooth, shiny, dome-shaped with central umbilication; viral warts are verrucous (rough/keratotic) and lack umbilication.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why should a solitary umbilicated papule in an adult be examined carefully?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because a solitary umbilicated papule can mimic a basal cell carcinoma, which must be excluded, especially in an older adult with a single lesion rather than typical clustered molluscum.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Which infections can mimic molluscum in a patient with HIV?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Disseminated cutaneous cryptococcosis and histoplasmosis can produce umbilicated papules mimicking molluscum, which is an important consideration in advanced HIV.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What are viral warts (verrucae) and what causes them?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Common, benign epidermal growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV infects keratinocytes and drives their proliferation and hyperkeratosis, producing rough, papillomatous ('warty') keratotic lesions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why do warts have a rough, warty, papillomatous surface?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because HPV infection of epidermal keratinocytes drives keratinocyte proliferation and hyperkeratosis, producing the characteristic rough, cauliflower-like papillomatous surface.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the natural history of most viral warts?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Most are self-limiting and clear spontaneously through cell-mediated immunity, often within 1–2 years (especially in children), so treatment is often optional.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How do viral warts spread, and who is predisposed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: By direct contact and autoinoculation. They favour children, moist/traumatised skin, and the immunocompromised.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe a common wart (verruca vulgaris) and its usual site/HPV types.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A firm, keratotic, papillomatous 'warty' papule with a rough surface, typically on the hands, fingers and knees. Usually HPV types 2 and 4.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe a plantar wart (verruca) and its features.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: An inward-growing, often painful (on weight-bearing) wart on the sole, showing black dots (thrombosed capillaries) and disruption of the skin lines. Usually HPV type 1.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe plane (flat) warts.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Small, flat-topped, smooth papules, often multiple, on the face and hands. They Koebnerise (spread in a line from scratching). Usually HPV types 3 and 10.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe a filiform wart.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A thread-like, finger-like projection, typically on the face and neck. Usually HPV type 2.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe genital warts (condylomata acuminata) and their HPV types.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Soft, fleshy, papillomatous lesions in the anogenital area, usually caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What key clinical clue distinguishes a plantar wart from a corn/callus?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A wart DISRUPTS the normal skin lines (dermatoglyphics) and shows tiny black dots (thrombosed capillaries) on paring, and is painful on pinching. A corn/callus PRESERVES the skin lines, has no black dots, and is painful on direct pressure.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What are the 'black dots' seen in warts?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Thrombosed capillaries within the wart, visible especially on paring — a useful diagnostic clue that helps distinguish a wart from a callus/corn.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Which low-risk HPV types cause benign genital warts?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: HPV 6 and 11.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Which high-risk (oncogenic) HPV types are important, and what cancers do they cause?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: HPV 16 and 18 — associated with cervical cancer and also anal, penile, vulval and oropharyngeal cancers, as well as Bowen's disease/SCC (especially genital/digital and in the immunosuppressed).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How does the oncogenic HPV link underpin public health measures?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: High-risk HPV (16/18) causing cervical and other cancers is the basis of cervical screening (HPV testing) and the HPV vaccine, which covers HPV 6 and 11 plus high-risk types including 16 and 18.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How are viral warts usually diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Clinically, from the characteristic warty lesion with disrupted skin lines ± black dots. Investigation (STI screen, biopsy) is reserved for anogenital warts or atypical/persistent/suspicious lesions.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: When should a wart-like lesion be biopsied?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: If it is atypical, persistent, or suspicious for malignancy — particularly a solitary keratotic lesion enlarging or ulcerating in an adult, or in the immunosuppressed, to exclude SCC.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the first-line topical treatment for troublesome common/plantar warts?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Topical salicylic acid (a keratolytic, applied over weeks), often combined with cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen). Duct-tape occlusion and curettage/cautery are other options.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why should plane/facial warts be treated gently?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: To avoid scarring — aggressive treatments like cryotherapy or curettage can cause scarring on the face; gentle approaches are preferred.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How are genital warts treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Topical podophyllotoxin or imiquimod, or cryotherapy/ablation, along with sexual health referral and STI screening.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why do the immunosuppressed warrant a lower threshold to treat/biopsy warts?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Because their warts are more numerous and persistent and carry a higher malignancy risk (HPV-related SCC), so treatment, monitoring and biopsy of suspicious lesions are more readily undertaken.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Is doing nothing a valid option for viral warts?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Yes — since most warts clear spontaneously (immune clearance, often within ~2 years, especially in children), observation/reassurance is a valid management option when the wart is not troublesome.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is impetigo and what organisms cause it?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A common, contagious, SUPERFICIAL bacterial skin infection — usually Staphylococcus aureus (± Streptococcus pyogenes) — classically producing a red lesion with a golden/honey-coloured crust, often on the face of children.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the hallmark lesion of (non-bullous) impetigo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A golden/honey-coloured CRUST on an erythematous base (from ruptured vesicles/pustules), classically perioral/nasal and on the face.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How does impetigo typically enter the skin?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Staph/strep colonise and infect the superficial epidermis, often through a small break in the skin — a scratch, insect bite, or eczema.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What are the two forms of impetigo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
• Non-bullous impetigo (commonest, golden honey-coloured crusts)
  • and bullous impetigo (fluid-filled blisters/bullae that rupture to a thin brown crust)

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What causes bullous impetigo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Staphylococcus aureus EXFOLIATIVE TOXIN — the same toxin as in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), but acting locally at the infection site.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Explain the link between bullous impetigo and SSSS.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Both are caused by the same Staph aureus exfoliative toxin (which cleaves desmoglein-1). Bullous impetigo = LOCALISED (toxin acts at the infection site); SSSS = WIDESPREAD (toxin spreads via the bloodstream).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Describe the lesions and sites of bullous impetigo.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Flaccid, fluid-filled blisters (bullae) that rupture to leave a thin 'collarette' of scale and brown crust, with the mucosa spared. Sites include trunk and flexures; often affects infants/neonates.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Who most commonly gets impetigo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Young children (typically 2–5 years) — it is the commonest bacterial skin infection in this age group. Bullous impetigo often affects infants/neonates.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How does impetigo spread?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: It is very contagious — spread by direct contact and autoinoculation (producing new lesions). It may cause regional lymphadenopathy but children are usually not systemically unwell.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is impetigo usually diagnosed, and when is a swab indicated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Clinically, from the golden crusts. A swab for MC&S is indicated if the infection is recurrent, widespread, fails treatment, MRSA is suspected, or there is an outbreak.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is the first-line treatment for LOCALISED non-bullous impetigo (not systemically unwell), per NICE?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Hydrogen peroxide 1% cream, 2–3 times daily for 5 days — an antibiotic-sparing first-line option.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Why does NICE recommend hydrogen peroxide 1% first-line for localised impetigo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: For antibiotic stewardship — to reduce antibiotic resistance (especially rising fusidic acid resistance) rather than jumping straight to a topical antibiotic.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is used if hydrogen peroxide is unsuitable (e.g. around the eyes) or ineffective for localised impetigo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Topical fusidic acid 2% three times daily for 5 days; mupirocin is used if fusidic acid resistance is suspected.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is widespread non-bullous impetigo treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: With a topical OR oral antibiotic (rather than hydrogen peroxide alone).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How is bullous impetigo, or impetigo in a systemically unwell/high-risk patient, treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: An ORAL antibiotic — flucloxacillin first-line (adults 500 mg four times daily for 5 days, extendable to 7); clarithromycin (adults 250–500 mg twice daily for 5 days) if penicillin-allergic, or erythromycin in pregnancy. A systemically unwell child, and any infant under 1 year with bullous impetigo, also needs assessment for admission and specialist advice.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What oral antibiotic is first-line for impetigo, and the alternative if penicillin-allergic?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Flucloxacillin first-line — adults 500 mg four times daily for 5 days (up to 7 if needed). If penicillin-allergic: clarithromycin 250–500 mg twice daily for 5 days, or erythromycin in pregnancy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What hygiene and school-exclusion advice applies to impetigo?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Don't touch/scratch lesions or share towels, and wash hands. Stay off school/nursery until the lesions are healed/crusted over OR until 48 hours after starting antibiotics.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: List the recognised complications of impetigo.
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back:
• Impetiginised eczema
  • cellulitis (deeper spread)
  • ecthyma (a deeper, ulcerated form that can scar)
  • and SSSS (from the bullous/toxin form)
Spreading erythema with fever, a rapidly advancing margin, or pain out of proportion to the visible signs means reconsidering necrotising fasciitis and escalating within the hour.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: Which post-streptococcal complication can follow streptococcal impetigo, and which does NOT occur?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis can rarely follow strep impetigo; rheumatic fever does NOT follow skin strep (unlike throat strep infection).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: What is ecthyma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: A deeper, ulcerated form of impetigo that extends through the epidermis into the dermis and can heal with scarring.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.front: How can impetigo be distinguished from eczema herpeticum?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Infections.back: Impetigo shows golden/honey-coloured crusts and children are usually well; eczema herpeticum (HSV) shows monomorphic 'punched-out' vesicles/erosions with systemic upset and is an emergency requiring aciclovir.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What are the common skin malignancies and pre-malignant lesions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: The common skin malignancies — BCC, SCC and melanoma — together with pre-malignant lesions (actinic keratosis, Bowen's disease) and melanoma in situ (lentigo maligna); most are UV-driven.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the organising principle for skin cancers?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Split into non-melanoma (BCC, SCC) vs melanoma — BCC = commonest, locally invasive, rarely metastasises; SCC = can metastasise, arises in sun-damaged skin/AK/Bowen's; melanoma = most dangerous (assess with ABCDE; Breslow thickness = key prognostic factor).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the key referral rule across skin lesions?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Any changing, non-healing or ABCDE-positive lesion → urgent (2-week-wait) dermatology referral (with emphasis on sun protection and surveillance) — though BCC is usually a routine referral.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is a basal cell carcinoma (BCC, 'rodent ulcer')?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: The COMMONEST skin cancer — a locally invasive, slow-growing malignancy of the basal keratinocytes, driven by cumulative UV; the classic lesion has a rolled (pearly) edge, central ulcer and telangiectasia.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the 'core concept' of BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Locally invasive but almost NEVER metastasises — dangerous through local destruction (erodes tissue, hence 'rodent ulcer'), not distant spread → low-mortality but high-morbidity (neglected facial BCC invades cartilage/bone/eye/nose).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What are the classic recognition features of a BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back:
• A rolled, 'pearly' (translucent/shiny) border (the hallmark)
  • central ulceration/crusting ('rodent ulcer')
  • and fine surface telangiectasia
  • it can be pigmented (a melanoma mimic).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the commonest BCC subtype, and its appearance?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Nodular BCC — the classic pearly, rolled-edged papule + telangiectasia ± central ulcer.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is a superficial BCC, and how is it treated?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A flat, scaly, erythematous plaque (often on the trunk) — amenable to topical treatment/photodynamic therapy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is a morphoeic (sclerosing/infiltrative) BCC, and why does it matter?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A scar-like BCC with ill-defined margins → HIGH-RISK (deeper, harder to clear → Mohs surgery).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is a pigmented BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A pigmented variant that mimics melanoma.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the main driver and who is at risk of BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Cumulative UV (sunburn, sunbeds); fair skin (Fitzpatrick 1–2), older age and outdoor occupation.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What other (non-UV) risk factors predispose to BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back:
• Immunosuppression (transplant)
  • radiotherapy
  • arsenic
  • and genetic syndromes — Gorlin (basal cell naevus) syndrome (multiple/young BCCs) and xeroderma pigmentosum.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What should multiple or young-onset BCCs make you consider?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Gorlin (basal cell naevus) syndrome.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: How is BCC diagnosed?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back:
• Clinically (± dermoscopy), confirmed histologically
  • a diagnostic incisional/punch biopsy may be taken first to determine the growth pattern (subtype) before definitive excision (especially for larger/high-risk lesions)
  • CT/MRI only for suspected deep invasion (bone/nerve/orbit).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the referral pathway for a suspected BCC (NICE)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Usually a ROUTINE referral (slow-growing, rarely metastasises — NOT routinely 2-week-wait); consider 2-week-wait ONLY if delay would have significant impact (critical site — near eye/nose — or large size).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Which skin cancers get a 2-week-wait referral, and which is the exception?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: SCC and melanoma → 2-week-wait; BCC is the exception (usually routine).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the treatment of choice for BCC, and the excision margins?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Surgical excision — ~4 mm margin (low-risk), ≥5 mm (high-risk).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: When is Mohs micrographic surgery used for BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: For high-risk BCC — facial/cosmetic sites, recurrent lesions, morphoeic/infiltrative subtypes, or ill-defined margins (staged, real-time margin control).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What non-surgical options exist for BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back:
• Curettage + cautery and radiotherapy (if surgery is unsuitable/declined)
  • for the superficial subtype — photodynamic therapy, imiquimod, topical 5-fluorouracil and cryotherapy.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the follow-up advice for an adequately-excised isolated BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Do NOT routinely follow up — advise sun protection + self-monitoring; follow up high-risk/multiple/incompletely-excised BCCs.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Does BCC commonly metastasise?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: No — it is locally invasive but rarely metastasises; the danger is local tissue destruction.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: The second commonest skin cancer — a malignancy of the epidermal KERATINOCYTES, UV-driven, presenting as an exophytic, rapidly-growing, keratotic nodule on sun-exposed skin, often arising in a pre-existing actinic keratosis or Bowen's disease.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the 'core concept' of SCC (the key distinction from BCC)?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: SCC CAN METASTASISE (BCC essentially doesn't) → the more dangerous keratinocyte cancer, needing more urgent handling (2-week-wait).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What are the three organising threads of SCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back:
• (1) A UV-damage spectrum (actinic keratosis → Bowen's → invasive SCC)
  • (2) recognise high-risk features
  • (3) 2-week-wait + excision.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: Where does SCC typically occur?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: On the face, lips, ears, hands and limbs — in older, fair-skinned, sun-damaged patients.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: How does SCC differ from BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: SCC: rapid growth (weeks), keratotic/scaly/crusted/exophytic, ulcerates, often tender/painful and bleeds, CAN metastasise (lymph nodes), arises from actinic keratosis/Bowen's → 2-week-wait. BCC: slow (months–years), pearly/rolled edge/telangiectasia, usually asymptomatic, rarely metastasises → routine.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the single most important distinction between SCC and BCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Metastatic potential — SCC can metastasise (regional lymph nodes); BCC rarely does.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is an actinic (solar) keratosis?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A PRE-cancerous, scaly, erythematous 'sandpaper' patch on sun-exposed skin in the elderly, with a small risk of progression to SCC.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is the UV-damage spectrum leading to invasive SCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: Actinic keratosis (pre-cancer) → Bowen's disease (SCC in situ) → invasive SCC.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: How are the SCC precursors treated to prevent SCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back:
• Topical 5-fluorouracil/imiquimod/diclofenac
  • cryotherapy
  • photodynamic therapy and curettage.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What are the clinical features of an SCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: An enlarging scaly/crusted lump growing rapidly over weeks, which may ulcerate and is often tender/painful and bleeds, arising in pre-existing actinic keratosis/Bowen's on sun-exposed sites (face, lips, ears, hands, limbs).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is a keratoacanthoma?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: A rapidly-growing crateriform nodule with a central keratin plug — a well-differentiated SCC variant (treat as SCC).

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What is a Marjolin's ulcer?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back: An SCC arising in a chronic wound/scar/ulcer/burn.

conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.front: What are the risk factors for SCC?
conditions__DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & P.back:
