investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: Patch test reactions are delayed, so a second reading at day 4 (72–96 h) is essential — some positives only appear at this later reading, and stopping at day 2 risks a false-negative conclusion. Systemic steroids would suppress the reaction and cause false negatives, and skin-prick testing assesses a different (Type I) mechanism.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A patient with facial eczema has a strongly positive patch test to nickel. However, they have no history of nickel exposure to the face and the eyelid rash is worst. What is the single most important principle in interpreting this result?
options: Any positive patch test confirms the cause and warrants total nickel avoidance
A positive nickel test always indicates an irritant, not allergic, reaction
The result must be judged for clinical relevance against the patient's exposure and rash distribution
Nickel positivity excludes all other allergens as the cause
The test should be repeated with skin-prick testing to confirm
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: The result must be judged for clinical relevance against the patient's exposure and rash distribution
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: A positive patch test is only meaningful if it is clinically relevant — it must fit the patient's exposure history and the distribution of dermatitis. Here nickel positivity does not explain an eyelid-predominant rash, so other allergens (e.g. cosmetics, preservatives, MI in wipes) should be considered. Skin-prick testing is inappropriate as it detects Type I, not Type IV, hypersensitivity.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A 52-year-old man is referred with a 9 mm asymmetric, irregularly pigmented lesion on his back that has recently changed. Which is the most appropriate initial biopsy to establish the diagnosis?
options: Shave biopsy of the raised area
Incisional biopsy of the darkest part
4 mm punch biopsy of the centre
Curettage and cautery of the lesion
Excisional biopsy with a 2 mm margin including a cuff of subcutaneous fat
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: Excisional biopsy with a 2 mm margin including a cuff of subcutaneous fat
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: Suspected melanoma is diagnosed by complete excisional biopsy with a narrow 2 mm margin, so the whole lesion is available to measure Breslow thickness accurately. Shave, incisional, punch or curettage approaches sample only part of the lesion, can transect the tumour and under-stage the Breslow depth, so they are avoided.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A pathology report on an excised cutaneous melanoma is being discussed at the MDT. Which single feature is the most important prognostic factor and the main driver of definitive surgical margins?
options: Diameter of the lesion in millimetres
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: Breslow thickness — the vertical depth from the top of the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell — is the single most important prognostic factor in primary cutaneous melanoma and drives the wide local excision margin and staging. Clark level is now largely superseded, and while subtype, regression and diameter are recorded, none is the principal prognostic determinant.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: An excisional biopsy confirms a melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1.6 mm. Approximately what wide local excision margin is most appropriate at definitive surgery?
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: WLE margins are guided by Breslow thickness (approximate values): melanoma in situ ~0.5 cm, <1 mm ~1 cm, 1–2 mm ~1–2 cm, and >2 mm ~2 cm. A 1.6 mm melanoma therefore warrants an approximate 1–2 cm margin. No further excision would leave inadequate clearance, 0.5 cm is for in situ disease, and 4 cm or amputation are excessive.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A 52-year-old man has a melanoma excised from his back. Histology shows a Breslow thickness of 1.6 mm with no ulceration. Examination of the regional nodal basins is normal and nodal ultrasound is negative. What is the main purpose of offering him a sentinel lymph node biopsy?
options: To stage the disease by detecting subclinical nodal micrometastasis
To surgically clear all involved nodes and improve overall survival
To obtain tissue to confirm the primary diagnosis of melanoma
To directly treat established palpable nodal metastases
To screen for distant visceral metastases
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: To stage the disease by detecting subclinical nodal micrometastasis
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: SLNB is a staging/prognostic procedure in clinically node-negative intermediate-thickness melanoma (Breslow >0.8–1.0 mm). It samples the first draining node to detect micrometastasis and refine prognosis; it is not itself therapeutic, does not establish the primary diagnosis (that is the excisional biopsy), and does not detect distant disease.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A patient with a newly diagnosed melanoma is due to have a sentinel lymph node biopsy. Which combination of methods is used to localise the sentinel node?
options: Whole-body PET-CT followed by open node dissection
Technetium-99m colloid with lymphoscintigraphy, patent blue dye and a gamma probe
Palpation alone with excision of the largest node
MRI lymphangiography and methylene blue tattoo
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: Technetium-99m colloid with lymphoscintigraphy, patent blue dye and a gamma probe
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: The sentinel node is localised using a radiolabelled tracer (technetium-99m colloid) with pre-operative lymphoscintigraphy, intra-operative patent blue dye, and an intra-operative hand-held gamma probe. The 'hot and blue' node(s) are then excised for histology.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A 60-year-old woman with a previously excised melanoma is found to have a firm, palpable, biopsy-proven metastatic lymph node in the ipsilateral groin. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Sentinel lymph node biopsy at the primary site
Repeat wide local excision of the scar only
Cross-sectional staging imaging and therapeutic lymph node dissection
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: Cross-sectional staging imaging and therapeutic lymph node dissection
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: SLNB is only for clinically and radiologically node-negative patients. Clinically palpable or biopsy-proven nodal disease is beyond the remit of SLNB — the patient needs staging imaging (CT/PET) and a therapeutic lymph node dissection, with consideration of systemic/adjuvant therapy.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A 68-year-old woman has a shallow, exudative ulcer over the medial malleolus with surrounding haemosiderin staining, consistent with a venous ulcer. Before starting treatment, which investigation is essential?
options: Immediate application of four-layer compression bandaging
Ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) with a hand-held Doppler
Punch biopsy of the ulcer edge
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: Ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) with a hand-held Doppler
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: ABPI must be measured before compression to exclude significant PAD, because compressing an ischaemic limb can cause necrosis. Compression should not be applied until arterial disease is excluded (ABPI >=0.8).

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A patient with a venous-appearing leg ulcer has an ABPI of 0.6. What is the most appropriate management regarding compression?
options: Double the compression to overcome the arterial disease
Withhold compression and obtain vascular input before any compression
Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: Withhold compression and obtain vascular input before any compression
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: ABPI <0.8 indicates a significant arterial component. Full high compression is unsafe; the patient needs vascular assessment, and any compression (reduced/modified) should only be under specialist guidance.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD has a leg ulcer and an ABPI of 1.4. Which statement is correct?
options: The value is likely falsely elevated by calcified vessels and is unreliable
The high value confirms the limb is well perfused and safe for compression
This confirms severe arterial disease requiring amputation
Compression should be applied at maximal pressure
The Doppler machine is faulty and no further action is needed
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: The value is likely falsely elevated by calcified vessels and is unreliable
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: In diabetes and CKD, arterial calcification makes vessels incompressible, giving a falsely high ABPI (>1.3). The result cannot be trusted to indicate a safe limb; consider toe pressures/TBPI or duplex and seek vascular assessment.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A renal transplant recipient has a biopsy-confirmed cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip. Compared with a basal cell carcinoma, what additional step is most important?
options: Assessment of regional lymph nodes because SCC can metastasise
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.answer: Assessment of regional lymph nodes because SCC can metastasise
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: Unlike BCC (which essentially never metastasises), SCC can spread to regional nodes — especially with high-risk features (lip/ear site, perineural invasion, immunosuppression). Regional node assessment ± imaging/MDT is therefore essential.

investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.question: A patient has a recurrent, ill-defined basal cell carcinoma on the nasal ala. Which treatment offers the best margin control at this high-risk cosmetic site?
investigations__DERMATOLOGY__Biopsy & Sk.explanation: Mohs micrographic surgery gives complete margin assessment with maximal tissue preservation and is preferred for high-risk, recurrent or ill-defined BCCs at cosmetically sensitive facial sites such as the H-zone.
